item.title: You Don’t Need The Nuts To Overbet
item.dc:creator: Duncan Smith
item.description:

The post You Don’t Need The Nuts To Overbet appeared first on Upswing Poker.
item.content:encoded:
Most players only bomb the pot for value when they have the nuts, or at least very strong hands. It feels safe; after all, nobody likes looking foolish after firing a huge bet with one pair. The problem is that this mindset leaves lots of money on the table.

In a video from the Max Exploit Academy, available exclusively inside Lab 2.0. Avery “Playitsmart” Nitkin makes a simple but important point: overbetting is not about having the best possible hand; it is about how your hand performs against your opponent’s range. You don’t need the nuts to overbet for value. You need enough worse hands to call, and a reason to believe a big bet will earn more than a smaller one.

The rules Avery lays out are straightforward, but the way they connect makes them powerful. Here are the six lessons that stuck with me, along with a few of Avery’s own hands that illustrate the point.

1. If They Call Too Much, Go Thinner

The more often your opponent calls with weak hands, the thinner you can overbet for value.

Some players fold too much, making them excellent targets for overbet bluffs. Others call far too often, allowing you to overbet for value with hands considerably weaker than the nuts.

Example: Button opens Qs 9d versus a reg in the Big Blind. The flop comes 6h 2d 5s and goes check–check. On the Jd turn Hero bets 70% pot, villain calls. The river brings the Qh. Hero overbets 140% pot and gets called by Ks Js.

Top pair is not the nuts, but against a range weighted toward bluff-catchers it plays beautifully as a thin value overbet.

Takeaway: When villain’s range is heavy with bluff-catchers, extract as much value as possible.

2. The Less You Bluff, the Thinner You Value Bet

Sticky regs and recs who hate to fold are the players you least want to bluff, and the ones you should target with thin value.

If bluffing is unprofitable because someone calls too often with weak hands, you can respond by value betting thinner.

Example: Button opens Ah Td against a reg in the Big Blind. The action checks through flop and turn on 3s 8c 2c Qs. The river is the Tc. Villain checks, Hero bombs 130% pot, and gets called by 4h 2h.

Second pair top kicker is more than good enough when villain cannot fold bottom pairs, even on scary boards where flushes and straights could theoretically be present.

Takeaway: If you can’t bluff them, go for thin value.

3. Overbets Crush Fish and Non-Believers

This one ties into the previous point, but it’s worth emphasizing. Overbetting crushes recreational players and paranoid regs alike who pride themselves on “not getting bluffed.”

They convince themselves you are making a move, and they will call just to prove it. You can extract far more EV from them than you should normally be able to.

Example: Versus an Under the Gun reg open, Big Blind defends with As 8s. The flop comes 8d 7c 4c, Hero donks and gets called. The 9h turn goes check–check. On a 4d river, Hero fires 140% pot and gets called by Ah Jh.

Against a sticky fish who usually keeps betting his strong hands, the river check creates an opportunity to size up for thin value.

Takeaway: Against players who cannot fold, big bets are the simplest way to make money.

4. The Fewer Combos That Beat You, the Bigger You Can Go

Here’s where range awareness proves to be critical. When your opponent has very few combos that beat you, you do not need the near-nuts to bet big.

Players often scare themselves with “what if” thinking: What if they have the straight? What if they slowplayed the flush? But if those combos barely exist in villain’s range, you are giving up money by not sizing up.

Example: Cutoff opens Qh Jc, a fish defends the Big Blind. The flop comes 7c Tc Jh. Hero checks back because the fish is known to be aggressive. The turn is 6c, villain leads half pot, Hero calls. The river is the Th. Villain checks, Hero bombs 130% pot, and gets called by 7s 5s.

Our hand is far from the nuts, but against a sticky fish who broadcasts his hand strength on the river by checking, it is more than enough to size up and get paid.

Takeaway: Identify what combos are actually ahead of you, not the monsters under the bed.

5. Hand-Reading Makes This Strategy Work

Thin-value overbetting is not about mindless aggression. It is about recognizing when your opponent has enough weaker hands that will call a large bet.

The sharper your hand-reading skills, the more of these spots you will see. 

Example: Big Blind flats Jd 8d versus a reg open from the Small Blind. The flop comes 5d Ts 4h, check–check. The turn is 8h, villain checks, Hero bets 50% pot, villain calls. The river is the 4d. Villain checks, Hero bets 130% pot, and gets paid off by 6s 5s.

If this opponent usually bets his stronger hands earlier, his check-heavy line leaves a range weighted toward weaker pairs. If those pairs will call a large bet, Hero can overbet for thin value.

Takeaway: Better hand-reading unlocks more profitable overbets.

6. Overbets Mess With Regs’ Heads

This last point is less about raw EV in the hand and more about the long-term effect on table dynamics.

Showing down thin value after bombing the river can stick in your opponents’ minds. Some may respond by folding more; others may start calling lighter. The opportunity comes from recognizing how each opponent adjusts.

Example: Button opens Ks 8d, villain defends the Big Blind. The flop comes 6c Qs 8c, Hero checks back. The turn is 6s, Hero bets small, villain calls. The river 3h arrives. Hero bombs 130% pot, and villain pays with Ad Tc.

Villain just saw a thin value overbet with second pair, second kicker. If he starts calling too lightly, keep value betting thin; if he begins overfolding, look for more bluffs.

Takeaway: Showing thin value can change how opponents respond to future overbets. Watch for adjustments you can exploit.

Putting It All Together

The big misconception is that overbets are only for the nuts or very strong hands. Avery’s rules show why that philosophy can be improved upon.

  • If they are unbalanced, go thinner.
  • If you are bluffing less, value bet thinner.
  • Fish and sticky regs should be your favorite targets.
  • Count the combos, not the “what ifs.”
  • Hand-reading is the most vital skill in this strategy.
  • Overbets create long-term psychological pressure.

How to Practice This

The easiest way to start is by deliberately looking for one overbet spot per session that is not the nuts. Even if you do not take it, train yourself to spot it. That repetition builds confidence.

Reviewing hands helps too. Run filters for spots where you did value-bet the river for a standard size, or missed the bet entirely, then ask yourself: Which worse hands would call an overbet, and would betting bigger earn more than my usual sizing? More often than not, you will realize their range was capped and your hand was plenty good enough to go large.

The important part is breaking the mental habit of thinking overbets belong only to the absolute top of your range. Once you get comfortable pulling the trigger with strong but non-nut hands, the rest starts to fall into place.

Every home game has one player who’s sure he’s the best at the table. The problem is that everyone else at the table is sure of the same thing.

Today’s Cardle quiz settles it. Doug Polk hand-picks 5 poker hands every day, preflop and postflop, and everyone plays the same set. It’s called Cardle, it comes from Lucid Poker (the training app Doug founded), and it takes about five minutes. Free, with no account and no download.

Here’s how to read your score:

  • 90 to 100: Feared grinder. Send it to your group chat immediately.
  • 70 to 89: Solid. One leak away from crushing your game.
  • 50 to 69: You are guessing in a couple of spots. The breakdowns will show you which.
  • Under 50: Good news, you just found 5 hands worth studying.

How Cardle works

  1. Read the spot. Each hand sets up a preflop or postflop spot with the action on you.
  2. Make your play. Fold, call, or raise preflop. Check or pick a bet size postflop.
  3. Get it rated. Every decision lands somewhere from Perfect to Blunder.
  4. Read the breakdown. A short note on the solver answer and what Doug recommends in practice.
  5. Get your score. Each hand scores a percentage, with partial credit in mixed spots. Your 5 hands add up to a score out of 100.

item.content:encoded:
When life gives you lemons, you make lemonade.

And in tournament poker, there are a lot of lemons.

Being card dead for hours while blinds escalate, seeing a “nothing burger” flop after calling a 3-bet out of position, or investing chips over multiple streets only to completely brick in a spot where the right choice is to give up and lose on the river — the list goes on.

Hope you like lemonade.

In these instances, you’re trying to make the best of a bad situation.

And that basically describes what it’s like to play from the blinds.

A forced blind bet and being out of position to everyone else in the hand if you decide to see three cards makes for a situation that provides the most complex, aggressive and fun hands in poker.

Understanding what the blinds are and what their function in the game is will massively contribute to your improvement when playing from them. Something you’ll need if you’re playing to win in today’s games.

In this and the next article, you’re going to learn everything you need to know about playing from the blinds.

Blinds — A Necessary Evil

In The Theory of Poker, famed (and infamous) author David Sklansky explains that were it not for the blinds, you’d be correct to play extremely tight.

“All poker starts as a struggle for the antes. If there were no ante, there would be no reason to play.”

Forced bets like blinds (and antes) serve to loosen up the game since the players posting the blinds are blind to their hand.

By including them, you have something to fight for. Blinds and antes are the action drivers in poker.

It’s no surprise then that an essential metric measuring skill in poker is the bb win rate — how many big blinds you win over the long run.

But notice, these incentives aren’t free. They come at a cost to the players in the blinds.

Being blind to your hand and posting a bet torches money.

Forgetting skill and blind defense, the Big Blind (BB) starts with a 100bb/100 loss rate and the Small Blind (SB), who posts half a big blind, loses half that.

When you play from these positions, you are starting from behind.

You aren’t trying to find a winrate from the blinds. 

You’re trying to lose the least you can.

The Big Blind

Posting a full big blind every orbit adds up.

Of all the positions in Hold’Em, the biggest loss rates come from the BB.

It is the single most expensive position to play from.

If the BB starts at a 100bb/100 loss rate, why don’t you just fold versus an open?

When your opponent signals they have a hand worth playing, doesn’t calling with marginal hands just increase the losses?

Not exactly.

While posting the blind produces a long-run auto-loss, the price you’re being laid means many marginal hands become EV winners, helping to reverse BB’s (and SB’s) curse. After all, you’re just trying to lose less than 100bb/100 with many of these marginal hands.

More on this next.

The 3 Most Important Factors in Preflop BB Defense

Strong BB defense is a combination of math, positional awareness and risk management. Together, these three considerations provide a framework that you can use to approximate the right strategy whenever you’re playing.

Pot Odds

BB defense is a matter of good gambler’s math.

When your opponent min-opens, you are usually being laid about 4.5 to 1. Their min-raise (2bb) + the ante (1bb) + your BB (1bb) and the Small Blind (.5bb).

This means you don’t need a lot of equity to break even on your call, ~18% raw equity. Most, except the worst hands you’re dealt, have enough equity to call versus a reasonably constructed open-raising range.

In other words, you should fold rarely.

In 2026, it’s common knowledge to defend the Big Blind fairly wide. It’s well understood that you are getting such a good price versus a small raise that you should defend your Big Blind as much as possible.

However, what’s often overlooked is how changing the pot odds should change your defense.

In live contexts, it’s not uncommon to see 3x or 4x open-raise sizes.

Let’s say you’re playing a live tournament. It’s the 300/600/600 level.

You’re playing 30K effective stacks (50bb effective) and your opponent opens to 2k on the Button.

What should you do?

Here’s how you defend the BB against a 2.2x BTN open in this GTO solution from Upswing’s Lucid Poker solver.

Lucid Poker cEV strategy. BB v BTN 2.2x open-raise. BB plays an 83% continuing range.

Versus the standard open-size, you should only fold 17% of the time.

But your opponent went bigger in this case, raising to ~3.3bb. The price is much worse.

Forgetting equity realization, you now need 28.6% raw equity versus the 20% you needed facing the 2.2bb open size.

That means your whole range would see shifts — fold frequencies, calling frequencies and 3-bet frequencies.

The winningest BB strategy is going to account for the raise size and antes. Even a dead SB (no player in SB this hand) should affect your BB defense.

But that’s just one piece of the puzzle.

Villain’s Position

Where your opponent open-raises from matters.

BB defense isn’t only about pot odds but how your range performs against your opponents’ range postflop. Raw equity is one thing but equity realization is another.

To illustrate, let’s compare BB defense at 50bb effective versus UTG and versus BTN.

Lucid Poker cEV strategy. BB v UTG 2.2x open-raise at 50bb effective. BB calls 51%, 3-bets 5%, and folds 44%.

Lucid Poker cEV strategy. BB v BTN 2.2x open-raise at 50bb effective. BB calls 66%, 3-bets 17% total, folds 17%.

Versus the same raise size, getting the same price, BB plays significantly tighter when playing versus UTG.

Why?

Because UTG’s range is much stronger. Take a look.

Lucid Poker cEV strategy. 50bb effective UTG raise-first-in chart. UTG raises to 2.2x with 17% range and folds 83%.

Lucid Poker cEV strategy. 50bb effective BTN raise-first-in chart. BTN raises to 2.2x with 53% range and folds 47%.

That UTG’s opening range is much tighter than BTN’s probably doesn’t come as a surprise to you.

However, what’s often overlooked is that villains’ range morphology (the shape of the range) has a significant effect on yours.

The stronger the opening range, the better equity realization you need to defend profitably.

  • Playing offsuit combos like Q9o versus UTG is bad for two reasons. First, your hand doesn’t play very well postflop versus a range that feels comfortable c-betting flops and turns. Second, when you make your hand, you are in danger versus UTG’s dominating hands.
  • When playing versus the BTN, even though a hand like Q9o doesn’t play very well postflop, your opponents’ range is wide enough that when you make a pair or a draw, you are in much better shape and able to get to the river more often.

Pot odds are a great starting point for figuring out BB defense but insufficient to paint the whole picture. Villains’ position helps further define your best response. Even so, while these two factors will help fight the BB bleed rate, factoring the next consideration when deciding how to respond to your opponents’ open will meaningfully help your ranges’ definition.

Stack Depth

While position can equalize the merit of good pot odds, effective stack depth serves to equalize position.

This is because when you’re playing 50bb effective stacks, you’re not really interested in putting all your chips in with marginal holdings versus a strong range.

With 48bb behind, you don’t really want to get it in with a bad top pair for the ~5bb in the pot.

As stacks get shallower, this changes.

Let’s compare the BB versus UTG min-open at 50bb and 20bb.

Lucid Poker cEV strategy. BB v UTG min-raise at 50bb effective. BB calls 51%, 3-bets 5%, and folds 44%.

Lucid Poker cEV strategy. BB v UTG min-raise at 20bb effective. BB calls 65%, 3-bets 8% combined, and folds 27%.

Facing a shorter-stacked UTG, BB defends much wider, folding 17 percentage points less often. They call 14 percentage points more often and 3-bet 60% more frequently, even using the all-in button.

Since you are playing shorter, the 5-6bb in the pot on the flop provides an incentive buffer that allows you to stack off with less than the top of the deck.

For example, versus a 50bb stack on a K high flush draw board, you aren’t happy getting the money in with a T-high flush draw. But at 20bb? It’s much more forgiving.

At shallower stack depths, domination and the need to play three streets of poker (which help equity realization for many hand classes) fall down the list of priorities. Raw equity versus range becomes everything.

____________________________________________________________________________

This is the first part of a series on playing from the blinds. Next time, we delve into playing postflop from the BB.

To learn more about how sizing impacts your bottom line in poker tournaments, read: How to Defend Against Large Flop C-Bets in Poker Tournaments.

item.content:encoded:
Contrary to popular belief, preflop No-Limit Hold’em is not “solved”.

Not in the sense that we don’t have GTO sims for it, but rather because a lot of people just don’t play like it, especially in lower-level fields.

Does this mean that following the GTO charts is wrong? If your goal is not to be exploitable, it’s not wrong. If your goal is to maximize your profit, it certainly is.

So, in this article, I am going to break down how you should play when you’re up against Big Blind and/or Small Blind players who are too tight.

Spoiler alert: You’re not going to be playing GTO!

Let’s dive in!

The Quick Fix

I’ll get straight to the point so that if you are looking for something highly tactical, it’s immediately useful. Afterwards, I will explain in more depth so you can understand the reasoning behind your new optimal strategy.

We define an opponent who is playing too tight as a player who falls into one or more of the following two categories:

  • Folds too many hands
  • Doesn’t 3-bet with enough hands

This is all benchmarked against the GTO strategy as calculated by the CFR algorithm. We base everything off of those solved outputs.

So, against a tight player by our definition, you should expand your opening range way more than you expect.

If this is roughly our starting baseline on the Button:

And this is roughly how the Big Blind should respond against it:

But instead he is defending close to this:

(Roughly 5% less 3-betting and 3% more folding)

Then this is how you should actually be open-raising from the Button:

You should significantly more often, from 43.6% against a Big Blind playing well, all the way up to 63.6%. A 5% under 3-bet and 3% over-fold opens the door for you to RFI with impunity.

Full disclosure, this strategy generates “only” 2bb/100 extra just from the preflop adjustments alone. But there’s a hidden benefit here: by opening way more, you get into pots with this type of player much more frequently.

And why is that good? It’s easy: humans tend to have predictable, correlated patterns. A player who is tight preflop is almost always going to be tight postflop.

In the model above, the solver can only take advantage of the preflop leaks because postflop, the algorithm is unbounded again in BB’s shoes, which leaves no room for an edge to be generated. That is absolutely not the case in reality.

So while you only win an extra 2bb/100 preflop, you are going postflop with a bluff-heavy range against an opponent who will continue forfeiting the pot too frequently compared to the GTO solution.

That is compounded exploitation at work. And not only do you get that small 2bb/100 edge, you also get to apply it almost 50% more often, and win more postflop while you’re at it.

The Why Behind The Strategy

The decision whether or not to open-raise hinges on one concept: equity.

More precisely:

  • Equity – The share of the pot that you have as a fundamental mathematical law of the game
  • Fold equity – The share of the pot (or equity) that you can steal from your opponent

Equity

Every hand has a certain amount of equity preflop. Even the weakest hand possible, 72 offsuit, has a nearly 12% chance to beat the strongest hand you can get dealt, which is pocket Aces:

The more equity you have, the higher the expected value of a raise is. The opposite is also true.

Fold Equity

Whenever your opponent folds, he gives up his equity in the pot. His equity goes to 0%, yours goes to 100%. You win the whole pot immediately.

Whenever your opponent calls, he realizes some of his equity in the pot.

Whenever your opponent 3-bets, he makes you give up your equity in the pot with the bottom of your range.

When you have an opponent who folds too often compared to GTO, he gives up his pot equity too often.

What this means is that every hand in your range increases its share (or equity) of the pot, since they get to have 100% equity in the pot more frequently when the opponent folds. This means hands that otherwise have too little equity to open profitably can now do so because they steal more equity than they should be able to.

Conclusion

Since the Big Blind is offering too much free equity compared to what he should (through a combination of over-folding and/or under 3-betting), this artificially increases the equity of all hands in your range. This pushes hands that would otherwise not have enough raw equity to open-raise profitably above that 0 EV bar, thus creating an optimal strategy that revolves around open-raising trashier hands.

This effect is stronger the fewer players are left to act as the fold equity effect increases.

That’s all for this article! Hope you enjoyed it and that you learned something new from it!

‘Til next time, good luck, grinders!

What Is a Single-Board Bomb Pot?

Quick definition

A single-board bomb pot is a No-Limit Hold’em hand where every player antes before the cards are dealt. Preflop betting is skipped entirely, and the hand plays one flop, turn, and river like a standard hand from that point on.

It’s one of two common bomb pot formats. The other is the double-board bomb pot, which splits the pot across two separate runouts and is more often played as PLO (if that’s the version you’re facing, our double-board PLO bomb-pot strategy guide covers it). For the full rundown on antes and mechanics, see our bomb pot glossary entry.

The short version to remember going into the strategy below: with up to eight players anteing 3-5bb each, you’re often looking at a 24-40bb pot before a single postflop bet goes in, at a table where stacks are 100-300bb deep.

You’re playing a big pot against the whole table, including hands that would normally be folded preflop. 

Where You’ll Find Them

Bomb pots are mainly a live cash-game feature, run at the house’s discretion (frequency and ante size vary by room), though a growing number of online platforms are starting to build them in as a software toggle as well.

Why Bomb Pots Play Differently

Everything about standard preflop strategy, hand selection, position-based ranges, isolating weak players, is gone. Every player is in, with a 100% range, regardless of what they were dealt.

Range advantages disappear

In a normal hand, the preflop raiser typically has a range advantage, since they showed strength before the flop and the caller’s range is capped by comparison. In a bomb pot, nobody did anything before the flop, so everyone’s range is literally every hand in the deck. So the things that normally drive bet-sizing decisions (who has the range edge, who has the nut edge) stop applying on the flop. What’s left driving strategy is position, stack-to-pot ratio (SPR), and board texture, and of the three, SPR matters most.

Adjusting to SPR

The ante size sets your effective SPR for the hand, and SPR, more than raw stack depth, determines which hands you want to be continuing with. In a deep-stacked game with a small ante, a hand like a backdoor-flush-draw-plus-overcard can profitably see a flop because it has room to realize its equity over three streets. Shrink the SPR (bigger ante, shorter stacks at the table, or both) and that same hand loses most of its value. There isn’t enough room left for a backdoor draw to get there, while a hand like top pair gets more valuable, because it doesn’t need three streets to make its money.

Multiway math punishes non-nut equity

The more players who see the flop, the more often a decent-looking backdoor draw is actually dominated. Kh Th on Q-4-2 rainbow looks like a normal semi-bluffing hand in a heads-up pot. In an eight-way bomb pot it’s competing against Ah Xh, Kh Jh, and multiple live backdoor combos, and it’s far more likely to get raised off its equity by a short stack on the turn than to realize it. The takeaway: non-nut backdoor draws that look fine heads-up are often traps multiway.

Key takeaway

With everyone dealt a 100% range, the usual range and nut advantages disappear. Your strategy depends on position, SPR, and board texture. Play the hand by SPR, not by stack depth, and be extra wary of non-nut backdoor equity once more players are dealt in.

Flop Strategy: Small, Tight, and Linear

Because nobody has a range or nuts advantage, flop bets are usually under 33% pot at higher SPRs. Two reasons drive this.

1. Minimum Defense Frequency (MDF) is lower with more players in the pot

The more players who can continue against your bet, the tighter your own range has to be to avoid getting exploited, because each individual opponent only has to defend a small slice of their range to keep you honest. Here’s what that looks like across bet sizes and player counts.

Minimum Defense Frequency (average defend % required, per opponent)
Bet size 1 opp. 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
10% pot 91% 70% 55% 45% 38% 33% 29% 26%
25% pot 80% 55% 42% 33% 28% 24% 21% 18%
50% pot 67% 42% 31% 24% 20% 17% 15% 13%
75% pot 57% 35% 25% 19% 16% 13% 11% 10%
100% pot 50% 29% 21% 16% 13% 11% 9% 8%
150% pot 40% 23% 16% 12% 10% 8% 7% 6%
200% pot 33% 18% 13% 10% 8% 7% 6% 5%

Each individual opponent’s required per-player defend frequency drops sharply as more players are dealt in, which is exactly why a single big bet doesn’t work the way it does in a heads-up pot: you’re not pressuring any one opponent nearly as hard as you might think, because they can all fold and let someone else’s hand do the work.

2. A big flop bet can’t create a two-street game for the out-of-position player

In a normal hand, betting bigger out of position is one way to build a pot over two streets. In a bomb pot, it doesn’t work that way. The tool for building a two-street pot from out of position is a heavy check-raising strategy on the flop, not a bigger bet.

How to think about your range

Picture it top-down and linear. You bet the strongest combos first: sets, two pair, and overpairs almost always bet. From there, whether a given top pair or backdoor-draw combo bets depends on things like kicker strength and backdoor-suit specifics, and the bar for what counts as “strong enough to bet” gets higher, not lower, the more players you’re betting into. More live opponents mean a tighter value threshold for kickers and backdoor draws alike, not a wider one.

Advanced note: why OOP ranges read as capped

A check-call from out of position can’t be a bluff, while an in-position continuation bet always could be, so an out-of-position caller is effectively capped the moment they check-call rather than check-raise the flop. That’s a big part of why OOP play in bomb pots leans toward checking rather than leading or raising, and it’s the same “capped, mostly single-pair” read behind the river sizing decisions covered later in this guide.

Key takeaway

Bet small on the flop, usually under 33% pot, because MDF is lower as more players are dealt in, and a bigger bet doesn’t buy the pressure it would heads-up. Build your betting range top-down, and use check-raises rather than bet size to build a multi-street pot from out of position.

Turn and River Strategy

The more often a board “transitions,” meaning the relative strength of hands shifts, the more passively you should be betting into it, and the more a brick favors continued aggression.

As the flop aggressor, you should always have more made hands than draws in your betting range. That’s just how bluff-to-value ratios work. 

  • Turn bricks: bet bigger, more often. Your made hands stayed good; your range’s equity advantage held.
  • Turn completes draws: check more, size down. Your opponents’ calling ranges just picked up equity relative to yours.

A “brick” is board-specific, not universal

Compare two similar-looking flops.

Q-7-2 rainbow, no flush draws, no meaningful straight draws. The calling range here is mostly Qx, 7x, 2x, and backdoor flush combos. Relatively few turn cards meaningfully shift who’s ahead. This board transitions less than it might look like at a glance.

Q-9-2 rainbow, same texture on the surface, but now the entire J-T region completes straights (J-T for the open-ender; K-T, K-J and J-8 for gutshots), and 9x/8x pairs shift relative strength too. This board transitions far more than it looks like it should.

Teaching yourself to list out “which turn cards actually shift equity” for a given flop, rather than eyeballing “wet vs. dry,” is the practical skill here, and it’s exactly why Q-7-2 supports much more turn aggression than Q-9-2 does, even though both look dry on the flop.

Draws completing hurts the bettor more than the caller

As the original flop bettor, you typically hold more made hands than draws; the field calling your bets typically holds more draws than you do as the bettor. So any turn card that completes a flush or straight helps the calling range more than yours, and the more players in the pot, the more true this becomes. Practical result: play much more passively on flush-completing and straight-completing turns, and don’t assume a “safe-looking” offsuit card is actually a brick; check whether it completes anything for the range that called you.

Worked example: the triple-barrel framework

200bb effective, 3bb ante bomb pot (about a 24bb pot), Q-7-2 rainbow. Button has AQ, bets 25%, HJ and CO both call. The board is dry enough that the calling range is mostly Qx/7x/2x with some backdoor equity, so a blank turn (something like a 4) is genuinely good for the bettor’s range, and supports a bet size that sets up a river shove. Compare that to the same spot on Q-9-2: the calling range now includes plenty of straight draws, so far more turn cards are “bad.”

Reading river cards: the same framework, one street later

The “good for my range vs. good for my hand” question doesn’t stop at the turn. Picking the Q-7-2 hand back up: HJ folds to the turn bet, CO calls. On the river, a naked deuce is actually a good card for the bettor: it either counterfeits part of CO’s two-pair holdings or does nothing at all. A king or a seven, by contrast, is one of the worst river cards in the deck, either making trips or giving KQ two pair. These are two hands CO is very likely to be holding.

Sizing is dictated by how the caller’s range has behaved on the way there. CO called the flop and the turn without ever check-raising, which reads as a capped, mostly single-pair range with little trap potential; and that supports shoving strong value hands rather than betting a smaller size that’s easier for a wider range to call. A trickier river, where only a narrow slice of the range should continue, calls for a smaller, more targeted bet instead of a big shove for more than the size of the pot.

Key takeaway

Ask whether the next card shifts who’s ahead, on both the turn and the river. A brick keeps your range’s equity advantage intact, so bet bigger and more often. A card that shifts equity toward the calling range calls for checking more and sizing down, whether that’s the turn or the river.

Shallow Stacks Change the Math

Once effective SPR drops to roughly 0.8 or below, the equity threshold to get stacks in falls sharply. This is the point where a hand that would check the turn at high frequency when deep (say, AQ on a Q-T-x-8 runout) instead just shoves, pushing its equity against pair-plus-showdown hands and worse Qx rather than playing a more nuanced line. When sizing bets multiway, size to the shortest stack in the hand, especially if that stack can reopen the action against you while you’re holding a weak draw you’d rather just check.

Key takeaway

Once SPR falls to around 0.8 or below, shove hands you would check with deeper stacks. In multiway pots, size to the shortest stack still in the hand, not to your own.

Four Common Leaks

1. Over-continuing weak pairs with no backdoor equity

The classic example: a hand like 9x with no backdoor draw, facing a bet with uncapped ranges still to act behind you. It feels wrong to fold equity against a small flop bet, but weak pairs with no way to improve are exactly the hands that should be folding most often in bomb pots.

2. Playing weak draws aggressively

A hand like 9c 8c on 7d 5c 4c looks live, but multiway it’s a weak gutshot plus a low flush draw that rarely wants to build a big pot. Raising it risks running into better flush draws and getting stacked by hands that should have folded to a smaller bet.

3. Overvaluing straight draws

Straights are weak made hands and weak draws in bomb pots specifically because you can never make the unique nuts; someone else can always have the same straight, and the board is still likely to transition further (pairing, completing a flush) even after you make it. Even worse, you can get freerolled by running into the same straight that also has a flush draw that beats you. Treat straight equity as a hand that wants to see cheap streets, not build big pots.

4. Over-bluffing wide boards after check-raising

On a board like Q-9-2 two-tone, it’s tempting to fire the entire “obviously live” suited region on the turn after check-raising the flop. But because check-raising ranges are more polarized in multiway pots, the actual value combos in that range can be a handful, meaning a turn barrel across “everything that looks live” can badly overshoot the correct bluff-to-value ratio.

Key takeaway

All four leaks come from playing a bomb pot like a heads-up hand. Fold the weak pairs and weak draws you’d normally continue with, treat straights as thin equity rather than a hand to build a pot with, and keep bluff-to-value ratios honest after you check-raise.

Conclusion

Bomb pots reward players who can do two things well: think in terms of SPR instead of stack depth, and read how likely a board is to transition before deciding how hard to push. Neither is intuitive at first. Tight, patient play can feel wrong when there’s already so much money in the pot, but you still need to be selective about which hands you continue with.

item.content:encoded:
Passivity gets a bad connotation in general, and it’s for a good reason.

Passivity means accepting what happens without active response, initiative or resistance.

Do you think we would’ve gotten where we are as a civilization if we had passively accepted our ancient state of living? Absolutely not. We were aggressive about improving our individual condition, and that desire for prosperity accelerated the improvement in general living conditions in the last few hundred years.

But to achieve that, people had to take risks. They had to have initiative. They couldn’t just accept the situations as they were.

The same is true in poker. You have to have initiative and provide resistance to your opponents’ strategies if you want to profit.

With this in mind, in this article I am going to bring to light 3 situations where I consistently see players playing too passively.

I’ve selected these spots based on both data and personal observation, with some of these leaks happening at stakes as high as 1000NL online.

Let’s get started!

Spot #1 – Not Check-Raising Against Small C-Bets Enough

Flop check-raising is a cornerstone defense strategy, especially when it comes to facing small c-bets.

The only real weapon you have against people that consistently and aggressively c-bet using small sizes is to check-raise a ton. This strategy punishes the thin value-bets and aggressive bluffing that the small size allows for.

Here’s a quick look at how you should be check-raising against a small c-bet on a disconnected board like K84 rainbow:

You should be aiming to check-raise about 14% of the time here. And I specifically highlighted this T7s hand to showcase the kinds of hands that most people are missing from their raising ranges.

To reach this check-raising frequency you need to check-raise with a bunch of hands that are loosely connected to the board via backdoor straight draws and/or backdoor flush draws (like Ac 6c, Th 7h, Jd 7d, Jd Tc etc.) , as well as some of your gutshots, especially ones with a backdoor flush draw.

Now, I am not only arguing for you to start doing this because it’s GTO-approved, but rather because I’ve seen how strong players fail to defend loosely enough after they c-bet small.

This happens because, usually speaking, these small c-bets happen on fairly dry and/or disconnected boards. This forces them to c-bet and call with very speculative hands in order to prevent you from being able to exploit them by denying their equity too frequently.

Moreover, what often happens is that they don’t play a very well-balanced c-betting strategy themselves and they end up betting larger with value hands and thus end up having too many weak hands in the small size. This is not necessarily a mistake on their part, it’s actually quite defensible in many situations, but it is an aspect that you can take advantage of.

Now, there is an even better spot to fire these check-raises against small bets, and that is when the board is more connected and wetter. In those spots, where c-betting larger is often correct, the small size is actually much weaker and they will end up over-folding even more. Think of a board like Jd 8d 4s. A small c-bet there is almost always a hand with a capped value. You can check-raise and over-realize with your bluffs.

If you look closely here, you can see that the solver will mix a ton of strong hands into that 33% pot size (AA, KK, QQ, AJ, KJ, JJ, 88, etc.). That will simply not happen nearly enough in practice, and your opponent will end up with a lot more hands like Qs 6s, 7s 6s, Ks 9c, etc. that will end up folding against a check-raise. Do not let him realize equity like this. Punish him instead.

Spot #2 – Not Probe-Betting River Thin Enough

Now, it’s not all about bluffing you see. You can also be too passive with regards to extracting value.

Consider the following scenario. You defended the Big Blind against a Button open-raise with 8s 5s. The flop came Jd 8d 4s. You checked, he bet 75% pot, you called. The turn was the 4c. You both checked. The river came the 6s. 

You should NOT check here.

Now the reason why you shouldn’t check here is because what happens next is that your opponent will create a polarized betting range that will put your 8s 5s into a pure bluff-catching scenario. You will be playing a pure guessing game: is he over-bluffing or under-bluffing?

You have another option here: go for thin value and prevent yourself from facing a big bet.

Recognize that him checking back on the turn greatly diminishes the strength of his range since overpairs and better would continue barreling.

This means that you are holding a hand that is pretty strong, but not strong enough to put a big bet in. You can however bet small.

This way you accomplish two goals:

  1. You extract the value – always something we want to do
  2. You force him to create a proper raising range on the river – always hard to do

Most players fail to raise correctly on the river, which brings me to the final spot of this article.

Spot #3 – Not Raising River Block-Bets Thinly Enough

This is a mistake I see even at 1000NL online. The average player doesn’t go as thin for value as he should against block-bets.

Let’s quickly take a look at what the solver would do against that block-bet:

Even a hand as weak as JT should be raising here at a meaningful frequency. I don’t remember ever being raised with such a hand. In fact, I often see players just calling with a hand like QJ too.

What does this mean tactically? It means that you have free rein to start betting thinner for value, starting to add hands like 77 and Kd 6d. The whole reason why those hands didn’t want to bet was because they were getting put into a 0 EV scenario too often by the opponent’s aggressive, balanced raising. When that is taken out of the equation, value betting very thin becomes significantly more attractive than checking and hoping you make the right decision after.

Wrapping Up

Aggression wins. It is better to try and fail than to never try and never fail.

Will you make more mistakes by having an aggressive mindset? Yes. But what that also means is that, as long as you have a healthy feedback loop in place, you will learn faster and thus you will earn faster.

Take what’s yours and climb up the stakes.

Till next time, good luck, grinders!

item.content:encoded:
The river is the street where the gap between what you see in GTO models and what happens in reality is the largest.

GTO strategy is risk-neutral. You’re not.

This is the core issue that drives most of your mistakes.

In this article, I am going to break down 3 river mistakes you’re making and give you tactical insights to stop making them right now. The first two are about doing more while the last one is about doing less.

Let’s dive in!

River Mistake #1 – Not Bluffing Enough

I’ve studied databases for a long time and this is a pattern that consistently holds across time.

Your opponents are risk-averse. They tend to fold too much.

The problem is that you are also likely risk-averse when it comes to bluffing.

This means that your bias of under-bluffing is getting passively exploited by their bias of over-folding.

Am I arguing that you should start blasting off at every chance? Nope. But I want you to start doing more of it in a systematic, intelligent way.

I get it. Whenever you bluff, it seems like you’re risking a lot to win a little.

For example, you may be risking $75 to win a $100 pot.

The risk feels large relative to the reward. Not only that, but even if it’s a +EV bluff (works 45% of the time let’s say), it feels like it doesn’t work, because you’re losing more than half the time.

This is only exacerbated when we talk about overbetting.

In that case, you’re usually risking something like $130 to win the $100 pot.

Now it feels like you’re risking way more to win the same amount as before. You’d have a profitable bluff when the opponent folds >57% of the time. The frequency of folds that you get makes you feel like you’re winning more than losing. But when you lose, it feels much worse because you lost about 2.5x more than what you had already invested prior to the bluff.

Now, notice the emphasis on the word “feels”. That word doesn’t matter when we talk about math. The expected value (EV) equation doesn’t have a variable that contains what it feels like*.

I want to give you a pattern to start following.

Start consistently bluffing when your opponent has made an action or a set of actions that signaled that he has a weak hand.

Smaller bets lean weaker and so do double- and triple-check ranges. Start attacking those.

*Pro note: Am I saying that vibes don’t matter? Absolutely not. Intuition has a big place in any high-level player’s game. What I do want to bring attention to is that in order to achieve a very strong intuition, you have to sharpen it through tens of thousands of iterations at the poker tables and through off-table data analysis.

Without those, what you feel is not only irrelevant, but it’s biased in a way that hurts your win-rate. That’s because human nature is built around risk-aversion and survival.

River Mistake #2 – Not Bluff-Catching Enough Against Recreational Players

What do almost all recreational players like to do? They play loose preflop.

What that means is that they get to see the flop, the turn, and the river with a ton of weak hands.

They also don’t always like to showdown those hands, so they end up bluffing with some of them.

The problem that a lot of these players have is that, while they do bluff with their weak hands, they are usually too timid with their value. Betting with a hand that they know is likely good at showdown feels risky.

Risk-aversion kicks in again.

What if they get raised and have to make a tough decision? Checking and winning a lot at showdown feels safer.

What happens then is that their river betting ranges usually get skewed towards weak hands.

The thought process you use to evaluate a bluff-catch against a reg will not work as well against a recreational player.

They don’t see the game the same way regs do, so they don’t have the same river ranges. They also don’t value bet the same hands nor do they bluff the same hands.

Their style is random, yet predictable. Your job is to ignore the noise and follow the pattern. Click the call button more against them.

Pro note: I am not saying that you should do this against all recreational players. Some of them are really nitty and bluff-catching against them on the river will be very costly. Always use your best judgment.

River Mistake #3 – Calling Too Light After Being Multiway on the Flop

Multiway pots are a whole different beast.

The mathematics of the situation create a very different dynamic and a very different optimal strategy for all players involved.

The logic behind it is simple:

If bluffing was triggering people’s risk-aversion when up against one person, it compounds when there are more people involved.

Players start betting on the flop with fewer bluffs than they should, then drop off some more on the turn, and almost completely give up on the river.

If there is one spot where I want you to start being nitty with your bluff-catching, it’s this one..

Hands that are snap calls in heads-up pots become snap folds in multiway ones. Some of them even become snap raises.

Now, the thing that matters for you is that people are too nitty when it comes to betting in multiway pots.

Wrapping Up

Fixing your river mistakes is a sure path to improving your win-rate, as these pots are, on average, the largest and most exploitable. There is a lot of edge to be had here, so make sure you get yours.

I hope you enjoyed this article and that you learned something new from it. If you have any questions regarding these topics, please let me know in the comment section down below and I’ll do my best to reply.

‘Til next time, good luck, grinders!

item.content:encoded:
Do you play live poker? Then this one’s for you.

Garrett Adelstein is the most feared livestream player of all time. He started at the lowest stakes online and worked his way up to $1,000/$2,000 games in Los Angeles. Along the way, he became one of the biggest winners in live poker history. (He just released a memoir, Beneath the Cards, that covers the whole rise and the multiple falls along the way.)

On the latest episode of the Upswing Poker Level-Up podcast, Garrett sat down with Mike Brady and shared his 5 best tips for live cash game players.

Listen/Watch on Your Platform of Choice

Spotify Apple YouTube

You can also search “Upswing Level-Up” wherever you get your podcasts

 

 

Below is the quick version of each tip. Watch the full episode for the details, the examples, and the stories behind them. As Garrett puts it, “the devil’s in the details.”

WHAT’S IN THIS ARTICLE

  • Tip 1: Game selection is everything
  • Tip 2: Pay attention
  • Tip 3: Play hands against the biggest VIPs
  • Tip 4: Know the theory
  • Tip 5: Exploit, exploit, exploit
  • Bonus: Garrett’s $600,000 pot vs. Rick Salomon
  • Quick recap

Live Poker Tip 1: Game selection is everything

This one sounds obvious. But most players don’t take it nearly far enough.

During his rise, Garrett grinded the graveyard shift at Commerce Casino, 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. Why? Because overnight he could play short-handed against VIPs at $50/$100 or $100/$200 instead of 9-handed $10/$20 during the day. He was often making 10x to 100x more per hour.

You don’t need to move to LA to apply this:

  • Play in the best possible game. If there are 3 tables at your stakes, find the softest one.
  • Switch tables and seats as needed. Don’t stay put out of laziness or politeness.
  • Don’t lock up wins when the game is great. Maybe you can’t play until 7 a.m., but you can push until 2.

“I don’t care if I’m one of the best. What I’m supremely confident in is I’m one of the biggest winners in live poker history.”

Go deeper on Tip 1
Garrett’s full take on session length, when to quit, and the “poker politics” of bigger games.

Watch from 1:19 →

Live Poker Tip 2: Pay attention

“I know it’s difficult,” Garrett says. “But pay attention.”

Most live games are soft, and most live players are transparent. Every hand you watch is free information. Two things Garrett tracks most:

  1. When the big money goes in, do they usually have it? Lots of “decent regs” always have it when 100+ big blinds go in.
  2. When their line makes no sense, what does it mean? For okay players, a nonsense line almost always means a big hand. For VIPs, it’s often the opposite.

And here’s the counterintuitive part: study the weakest players the most. The worse someone plays, the more transparent they are, and the more value there is in watching them. Garrett didn’t review a single Doug Polk hand from his recent Lodge session because Doug plays close to GTO.

Live poker is slow. You only need to track 20-25 hands an hour. Put the phone away and watch.

Go deeper on Tip 2
What to look for beyond showdowns, including bet sizes, timing, and body language.

Watch from 6:08 →

New release Garrett Adelstein's new course See How Garrett Adelstein Destroys Live Cash Go inside Garrett's biggest pots and see the reads, exploits, and decisions behind his aggressive style. See what's inside →

Live Poker Tip 3: Play hands against the biggest VIPs

Tip 1 gets you into the right game. This tip is about building your preflop ranges so you play big pots against the weakest players and shut the strong players out.

In practice:

  • VIP in the pot and you’re in position? Isolate them and build the pot. They almost never fold preflop.
  • Strong player raises, VIPs behind you? Lean toward calling so the VIPs come along.
  • Hand is a mixed decision in theory? Pick the option that gets the VIP in the pot.

Mike pulled up the Lucid Poker Trainer for a 150bb button spot where hands like KTs, AQo, A5s, and 65s are all splitting between calling and 3-betting. Where the VIP sits at the table decides which way Garrett goes.

The principle behind all of it:

“When you’re playing against people you think you’re better than, make the pot as big as possible. The bigger the pot, the more expensive each of their mistakes will be.”

Go deeper on Tip 3
The full Lucid range walkthrough, how Garrett adjusts when the VIP is in the blinds, and why solvers overvalue suited connectors against weak players.

Watch from 12:15 →

Live Poker Tip 4: Know the theory

“This one’s going to be controversial,” Garrett warns.

You don’t need thousands of solver hours. But you need a baseline. If you don’t know the theoretically sound play, how will you know if, when, and how far to deviate from it?

Garrett learned this the hard way. When he started playing livestreams around 2017, players like Dan Zack and Art Papazyan were much stronger than him theoretically, and he couldn’t overcome that gap on exploits alone. Watching himself get outplayed pushed him to lock himself in his office and study for years.

The good news: you can skip most of that grind. His course, Destroy Live Cash, is built around simple heuristics that get you 80-90% of the way there.

If you’re crushing $1/$3 on intuition, you’re probably succeeding in spite of not studying theory. Add some theory and you only get better.

Go deeper on Tip 4
The full story of how getting outplayed on livestreams pushed Garrett to study, and saved his career.

Watch from 26:03 →

Live Poker Tip 5: Exploit, exploit, exploit

This has been Garrett’s bread and butter since 2004. Live poker is soft whether you’re playing $1/$2 or $1,000/$2,000, and live players don’t think you’re paying attention.

The process is simple:

  1. Find out what each opponent is up to (Tip 2).
  2. Build an attack strategy against each of them.
  3. Execute.

One warning: it’s a Goldilocks thing. Push an exploit too far, like showing up at showdown with a hand that’s way out of bounds preflop, and your opponents may catch on and counter-exploit you. Be ready to play the leveling game.

“You don’t need to be the best in the world at game theory. You don’t need to be the best in the world at exploits. But if you’re solid at both, you’re going to be a tough out.”

Go deeper on Tip 5
How far to push an exploit, and when to dial it back before your opponents catch on.

Watch from 29:46 →

Bonus: Garrett’s $600,000 pot vs. Rick Salomon

Garrett closed the episode with a hand from Beneath the Cards. It shows Tips 2 through 5 in action at the highest stakes he’s ever played.

The short version: Garrett has $300,000 in front of him. That’s roughly 80% of his bankroll. He 3-bets Rick Salomon out of the small blind, flops big, and by the turn nearly his entire net worth is in the middle.

We’re not going to spoil the rest here. Garrett walks through every street himself, including:

  • The read on Rick that told him not to slow down
  • Why he uses the same bet size with the nuts, a bluff, and everything in between
  • The run-it-three-times negotiation, and why a fourth board would have been a disaster
  • What the hand taught him about gratitude vs. entitlement in poker

Fair warning: it’s also a lesson in what not to do with your bankroll.

Watch the $600K hand
Garrett breaks down the whole hand street by street, in his own words.

Watch from 32:24 →

Take these tips to your next live session

Quick recap of Garrett’s 5 live poker tips:

  1. Game selection is everything. Play the best game, switch tables and seats, and don’t lock up wins when the game is great.
  2. Pay attention. Track lines and bet sizes, study the weakest players the most, and put the phone away.
  3. Play hands against the biggest VIPs. Use your preflop mixes to get into big pots with weak players and shut strong players out.
  4. Know the theory. You need a baseline so you know when to deviate.
  5. Exploit, exploit, exploit. Find each opponent’s leak, build an attack, and don’t push it so far that they catch on.

7

Deviations vs Elite Opponents
Hands 35-38 · 6 lessons
Exploiting bad players is the easy part. This section shows you how to find edges against pros who study as hard as you do, when a deviation is justified, and when to stop. It opens with the most expensive mistake in poker: exploiting in the wrong direction.

Hands 39-43 · 9 lessons

The Destroy Live Cash Framework
Know the GTO baseline. Find the exploitative deviation. Punish the mistake.

item.content:encoded:
The flop is the second most common node you will play (after preflop), and decisions here have big ramifications for how the rest of the hand plays out. Betting or checking, calling or raising with a certain hand means that you’re going to face an entirely different range on the following streets.

Not only does it affect your optimal strategy on future streets, but it also affects your opponent’s optimal strategy on the previous street as well. This means that flop mistakes can create preflop exploits for your opponent. That may sound unexpected, but I’ll explain why that is later in this article.

So, in this article, I am going to break down 3 flop mistakes you are likely making without knowing it and how they could be part of the reason why you’re not winning as much as you’d like.

Let’s get into it!

Flop Mistake #1 – Raising too infrequently

This one is really common, which is why I placed it first.

Raising or check-raising is mandatory if you want to play a really tough-to-beat strategy.

You can imagine raising as a counter-punch in boxing. Without frequent raising, you are basically a punching bag with a weak, predictable counter-punch mechanism attached to it.

If your opponent is smart and he understands that your counter-punching is very predictable (aka you tend to raise too value heavy), he will start hitting you with bets much more frequently, winning way more pots than he should, and realizing more equity at your expense, as he doesn’t allow you to see the turn for free as often, while he buys both the turn and river card for a cheap price.

If you implement an aggressive counter-punching strategy, your opponent will understand that he can’t get free shots and will be more tentative with his own aggression, allowing you to see more free turns and thus realize more equity.

If we go a level deeper here, if you’re playing against an elite-level player and he understands that you’re not going to check-raise him enough, for example, he will start making some preflop adjustments as well.

Not getting check-raised increases the expected value of a c-bet by a significant margin. This means that c-bet bluffing is higher expected value (EV) than you would expect. This further means that hands that were folding preflop, which often miss the flop, suddenly expect to generate more EV by bluffing on the flop. And since this is a high-frequency situation, this has a significant impact on the expected value of open-raising preflop.

Let’s take an example.

You open-raised on the Button and the Big Blind called. The flop comes Qd Jd 7s.

Here’s the EV of c-betting 33% pot compared to EV of checking back (in percentage of the pot being captured). Remember, the stronger the red color is, the better betting is relative to checking.

Now, villain’s GTO strategy in this spot is to check-raise 11% of the time against this bet.

Now here’s what happens to the EV of each hand if we strip some of the bluffs away.

Remember, the EV of checking hasn’t changed, only the EV of betting. We can see that the red color is now much stronger for the vast majority of hands, especially for the weakest hands.

Let’s compare the change for a trashy hand like Kh4h:

(before) (after)

We can see that this hand now wins ~0.8% more of the pot than it did in the GTO model, which, by the way, assumes no more mistakes on the villain’s end on the turn and river. That is completely unreasonable for a player who has this leak in his game.

Since the pot is around 5.5 big blinds right now, that translates to a gain of 0.045 big blinds per hand every time you see the flop. While this doesn’t seem like a lot, it allows you to expand your open-raising range to include hands such as these:

Flop Mistake #2 – Not Floating Enough

The second biggest mistake I see players make, and this is especially true when they play in position, is folding too easily on the flop.

I am talking about the weakest parts of their range here.

Let’s take a quick blind vs blind example. You open-raise in the Small Blind and the Big Blind calls. The flop comes Qc 8c 5d, and you bet 33% pot.

Their defense should include hands such as Ac 4h, Ac 3s, Kd 4d, Ah 7c, etc. K2-K7s, K9s, and A6o work their way in as well.

Take a look here, using Upswing’s Lucid Poker solver:

Not only should they be defending with them, they should be raising with them as well, which ties into the #1 flop mistake that I mentioned.

Not defending with these types of hands has two downstream effects.

The first order effect is that the Small Blind can simply start bluff c-betting a ton as an exploit.

The second order effect is that he can start betting on the flop and then easily check-folding on the turn with a large amount of his pure bluff-catchers. This happens because the turn stabbing range will simply be too strong. One of the functions of these weak floats was to balance the turn stabbing range. Without them, that range will be too face up.

Flop Mistake #3 – Checking Too Often with Very Weak Hands

This one is most common when playing in position, but happens out of position as well. It’s so common actually that I even see it at 500nl and higher online.

Let’s work off of an example to make it easier. Say you open-raised on the Button and the Big Blind called. You get dealt an Ad 8s 5s flop.

What is your first thought when seeing Kc 2c, or Qh 4h, or Qh 9d, or Th 9c?

You most likely have a bit of internal disgust and check back.

What if I told you that in this exact spot, these hands should be betting the majority of the time. Check it out:

Now, I just want to be super clear: This is not NECESSARILY a mistake.

If you have a very good reason, one that you could write out on a piece of paper, then it might very well be the best play.

These reasons could be:

  1. You’re playing against an aggressive calling station (over-raises and over-calls)
  2. Your opponent plays very well on the flop but folds to delayed c-bets too often
  3. Your opponent plays very well on the flop and turn but folds to the river double delayed c-bet

There are more reasons that could push this hand into the checking line as the highest EV line in practice, but if you can’t name the exact reason, then betting should be your highest frequency play.

I would argue that it is very likely that you are playing in games where c-betting all the time is optimal, and it’s because most of your opponents make mistakes #1 and #2: not check-raising enough and not floating wide enough.

If we look over what the optimal strategy is for the Big Blind, we will see that he needs to check-raise with roughly half of his gutshots and flush draws, all of his combo-draws, and a bunch of low pairs like 52s, 53s, 75s. He should also slow-play with his two pair roughly half the time.

Most of your opponents will be forgetting to check-raise with their low pairs, mostly lean towards check-raising with flush draws rather than gutshots, and will almost always check-raise with their two pair.

On the floating side, they will forget to check-call with hands like Qs Tc, or Js Td.

Conclusion

Poker is a game where, over the long run, everyone is dealt the same hands and the same boards. You both get the same amount of good hands and bad hands, good spots and bad spots.

Your edge lies in the difference between how you play each hand in each situation differently from how your opponents are playing the exact same situations.

Playing the strong hands correctly is easy. Playing the middling and lower parts of your range properly is where the edge exists because there are many more of them and the right strategy is harder to find and execute.

That’s all for this article!

‘Til next time, good luck, grinders!
